span.label: existence
span.quote: Speakers tend to repeat the syntactic forms of sentences in subsequent utterances that are minimally related in lexical, conceptual, or discourse content.

span.label: syntactic persistence in language production
span.quote: This involves the repetition of syntactic forms across successive utterances.

span.label: behavioural-experiment
span.quote: All of the experiments employed a syntactic priming paradigm that created a controlled analog of the situations that have revealed syntactic repetition in natural speech.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: syntactic (structural) priming: producing or hearing a sentence structure makes speakers more likely to reuse that same structure in a later, content-unrelated utterance - so syntax is represented and primed independently of meaning
span.quote: Speakers tend to repeat the syntactic forms of sentences in subsequent utterances that are minimally related in lexical, conceptual, or discourse content

span.label: it is unclear whether syntactic intrusions/perseverations can be accounted for in the same way
span.quote: In the case of syntactic intrusions or perseverations, however, it is not clear that the effects can be accounted for in a comparable way.

span.label: The null effect of the agency manipulation carries the usual indeterminacy of null results and may reflect a weak manipulation.
span.quote: The absence of an agency effect creates the usual indeterminacy associated with null results, leaving open the possibility that message factors may have had a less consistent impact than syntactic factors because the agency manipulation was weak.

span.label: The symmetry between syntactic and conceptual matching rests on unreliable differences and a very small item sample.
span.quote: But because the differences were unreliable and based on a very limited sample of items, this symmetry should be treated cautiously.

span.label: Both lines of evidence for the isolability of syntactic processing are described by the author as tentative.
span.quote: Two types of evidence for such isolability were found, although both must be regarded as tentative.

span.label: the filler items were tested on a schedule that reached 33, 78, 85 and 100 per cent by the end of each successive quarter of the list
span.note: eliminates: that recognition performance depends on how recently an item appeared rather than on the priming manipulation
span.quote: In every list, 33, 78, 85, and 100% of all previous filler items were tested by the end of each of the four respective quarters of the list.

span.label: syntactic persistence
span.quote: The repetition effect was found for two different types of sentences, with use of the alternative forms of each type (active versus passive transitives, and prepositional versus double-object datives) varying as a function of the form of a previous sentence.

span.label: priming effect
span.quote: Active and passive utterances each increased in frequency by 8% following corresponding primes.

span.label: lexical repetition
span.quote: However, lexical repetition does not seem to be a necessary component of the priming effect.

span.label: passive
span.quote: Active and passive utterances each increased in frequency by 8% following corresponding primes.

span.label: **THE EFFECT IS ON WHAT SPEAKERS CHOOSE, AND IT IS SYMMETRIC:** `Active and passive utterances EACH increased in frequency by 8% following corresponding primes.` Not a latency, not an accuracy - a shift in which of two grammatical options a speaker takes, in both directions equally. **The symmetry matters**: a bias toward one form would be explicable by that form being easier, and a bias toward whichever form was just heard is not
span.quote: Active and passive utterances each increased in frequency by 8% following corresponding primes.

span.label: **AND THE DEFLATIONARY READING IS CLOSED IN ONE SENTENCE:** `However, LEXICAL REPETITION DOES NOT SEEM TO BE A NECESSARY COMPONENT of the priming effect.` Prime and target share no words, and the effect survives. **This is the sentence that makes it SYNTACTIC priming rather than a long-range word priming** - and every other priming record in this corpus (meyer1971, neely1977, hutchison2003) is about exactly the relation Bock is ruling out
span.quote: However, lexical repetition does not seem to be a necessary component of the priming effect.

span.label: **IT MEETS lashley1951 ACROSS THIRTY-FIVE YEARS AND NEITHER CITES THE OTHER.** Lashley: `syntax is NOT INHERENT in the words employed or in the idea to be expressed` - argued from the impossibility of associative chains, with no experiment attached. Bock: syntactic form persists across utterances sharing neither words nor message. **The argument and the demonstration**, both merged into this corpus tonight, thirty-five years and one discipline apart
span.quote: The repetition effect was found for two different types of sentences, with use of the alternative forms of each type (active versus passive transitives, and prepositional versus double-object datives) varying as a function of the form of a previous sentence.

span.label: **AND THE STRATEGIC EXPLANATIONS ARE NAMED AND REMOVED:** `These variations occurred under conditions in which there was LITTLE OR NO IMPETUS for the active maintenance of the priming sentences in memory, or for the use of syntactic devices to create discourse coherence.` Not rehearsal, not cohesion. **The same move as marcel1983's second mask and erb2019's overlap control** - naming the alternatives and closing them rather than reporting the effect and leaving them standing
span.quote: These variations occurred under conditions in which there was little or no impetus for the active maintenance of the priming sentences in memory, or for the use of syntactic devices to create discourse coherence.

span.label: extends → activation-based theories of language production
span.quote: The advantage of the syntactic activation hypothesis is that it provides a unitary explanation for phenomena that otherwise seem quite disparate.

span.label: builds-on → the competition model of Bates and MacWhinney (1982; MacWhinney, Bates, & Kliegl, 1984)
span.quote: This view of linguistic rules as graded rather than fully determinate is comparable to that incorporated into the competition model of Bates and MacWhinney (1982; MacWhinney, Bates, & Kliegl, 1984).

span.label: extends → Levelt and Kelter (1982) and Weiner and Labov (1983) on repetition of syntactic form in natural speech
span.quote: A parsimonious explanation of these results, and those of previous investigations (Levelt & Kelter, 1982; Weiner & Labov, 1983), is that the production of sentences results in the activation or strengthening of the syntactic rules or procedures involved in their creation.

span.label: replicates → Experiment 2 of this paper
span.quote: The results thus replicated those of Experiment 2, but with a different cover task that encouraged fuller processing of the primes.

span.label: lexical repetition —distinct-from→ priming effect
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — **THE EDGE THAT MAKES THE PAPER SYNTACTIC.** `lexical repetition does not seem to be a NECESSARY COMPONENT of the priming effect` - both endpoints named, the relation is exactly non-inclusion, and it is the paper's own conclusion rather than a framing. Weight 0.95. **`distinct-from` is the right type here for once** - elsewhere tonight it has had to stand in for `co-occurs but does not cause` (mcmahon-olson2007) and lost half a sentence doing it; here non-necessity IS distinctness and nothing is lost. `seem to` is the authors' hedge and stays inside the quote.
span.quote: However, lexical repetition does not seem to be a necessary component of the priming effect.
